paras: The lynching of Jim Mitchell took place on the night of June 14, 1882, at Mount Sterling, Kentucky, where armed men took Mitchell, a Black man, from the jail and hanged him from a railroad trestle. Mitchell had been jailed that day, accused of assaulting the wife of a local farmer. The Louisville dispatch that carried the story across the country said the whole community approved of the lynching.

According to a special from Mount Sterling to the Louisville Evening Post, Mitchell waylaid the wife of Robert Thomas, "a respectable farmer," at noon on June 14 about two miles from town and assaulted her. The same dispatch described him as "well known about here as a vicious character" and said he was in jail within two hours. It added that the husband "went through the streets swearing" until the citizens' sympathy was roused so far that no one tried to stop what followed.

That night five men armed with pistols entered the jail and forced the jailer to hand Mitchell over. They took him half a mile from town and hanged him from a railroad trestle. The Hopkinsville South Kentuckian alone said the five men were masked. The next morning the coroner took the body down and buried it.

The dispatch said Mitchell had "confessed the crime twice" and that Mrs. Thomas had identified him, claims that come only from that report. No report of an inquest verdict, arrests or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage, and none of them was named.

The Louisville special ran on June 16 in papers from Wheeling to Savannah, Richmond, Memphis and Knoxville, under headlines such as "A Negro Fiend Promptly Lynched," "A Rape Fiend Lynched" and "A Brutal Rapist Lynched." The Wheeling Register headed it "Judge Lynch. His Decision and Execution Endorsed," printing the line that "everybody, even the negroes" justified the hanging. In Maysville, Kentucky, the Evening Bulletin ran the story as "Swift Vengeance" and said "Everybody fully justifies" the work of "Judge Lynch."

Western dailies such as the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Rock Island Argus and the Eureka Daily Sentinel printed a single line calling Mitchell "a ravisher" hanged "by a small mob." Weekly news digests over the following two weeks shortened the story further, calling the lynchers "armed citizens" or "armed men" and stressing that the woman was white. Kentucky weeklies, including the Bourbon News and the Semi-Weekly Interior Journal, ran brief local notices.

The Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic cited the case in an editorial titled "The Yankee Ku Klux," listing it with other recent lynchings to accuse Northerners who had condemned the Klan of hypocrisy. The Eaton Democrat in Ohio ended its notice with the remark "Thus, expenses stop."

Two Ohio weeklies, the Eaton Democrat and the Somerset Press, gave a different account, saying Mitchell was taken from the sheriff while being brought to jail by a mob of about 500 men. The Mount Sterling special and the Kentucky papers, closer to the event and earlier, all put the seizure at the jail and the number of men at five. Some digests dated the lynching to June 15, but the dispatches written on June 15 place it on the previous night, and the Wilmington Daily Gazette gives "Wednesday night," June 14. Several copies of the dispatch garbled the town as "Mount Harlan" or "Mount Herlin" and the victim as "Jim Michael."

reader.title: Lynching of Jim Mitchell
bases: Armed men took Mitchell from jail (or, in one version, from the sheriff) and hanged him from a railroad trestle over an accusation of assault (A3, A5, A22).

Every account says Mitchell was hanged by a group, five armed men in most versions (A3, A5) and a mob of 500 in two Ohio papers (A22, A23), without any legal process, as punishment for an alleged assault on a white woman (A7, A17).
The Louisville special (A3, A5), separate Kentucky items (A15, A16) and the Ohio version (A22, A23) agree that Mitchell was taken from custody and hanged at Mount Sterling, though they differ on how.

framing.detail: The Louisville special called Mitchell a 'brute' and 'wretch' and said everybody, 'even the negroes', justified 'Judge Lynch'; the Wheeling Register headed it 'His Decision and Execution Endorsed'.
Western and Northern dailies ran a one-line wire, 'Ravisher Hanged by a Mob'.
The Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic used the case in 'The Yankee Ku Klux' to charge Northerners with hypocrisy about lynching, not to condemn this killing.
The Eaton Democrat ended its item 'Thus, expenses stop.'

conflicts.note: The jail version comes from the Mount Sterling special and Kentucky papers, closer to the event; the Ohio version appears only in two weeklies a week later.
Short wires call it 'a small mob' (A1), consistent with five.
A11 redated the wire to June 16 so its 'yesterday' became the 15th; the June 15 dispatches put the lynching on the night of the 14th.
The variants occur in copies of the same dispatch and look like telegraph errors.
